analysis.one_liner: Suspends eight bee-harming insecticides until independent scientists find they won't hurt pollinators.
analysis.headline: The bill to suspend eight bee-harming insecticides won support from 80 House members — all Democrats — but never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the EPA to cancel the registrations of eight insecticides — including the neonicotinoids imidacloprid, clothianidin, and thiamethoxam — until an independent review board determined they would not harm bees and other pollinators. It would have barred new registrations for treated seeds and spray uses on bee-attractive plants, created a 15-member Pollinator Protection Board of scientists, beekeepers, and farmers to review pesticides, required annual government monitoring of native bee populations, and narrowed the emergency exemptions that let agencies use unregistered pesticides. It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Beekeepers and farmers who depend on pollination. The bill's own findings cite federal surveys showing beekeepers lost 35 to 46 percent of their hives each year between 2012 and 2018, and that pollination contributes about $24 billion a year to the U.S. economy. Anyone who eats fruits, vegetables, and nuts that depend on bees — one-third of North American food production — also stands to gain from keeping pollinators alive.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Beekeepers and farms that need pollinators

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to cancel the registrations of eight insecticides — imidacloprid, clothianidin, thiamethoxam, dinotefuran, acetamiprid, sulfoxaflor, flupyradifurone, and fipronil — until a new Pollinator Protection Board finds the chemical will not cause unreasonable harm to pollinators, based on peer-reviewed evidence and completed field studies.

Creates a 15-member Pollinator Protection Board made up of pollinator scientists, commercial, chemical-free, and hobby beekeepers, organic and non-organic farmers, and conservation representatives, with conflict-of-interest rules barring members who have ties to pesticide registrants.

Blocks the EPA from issuing any new registrations for seed treatments, soil applications, or foliar sprays on bee-attractive plants, trees, and cereals until the board has made its safety determinations.
Requires the Interior Department, EPA, and Agriculture Department to coordinate annual monitoring of native bee health and populations and report the findings to Congress and the public every year.
Narrows emergency-use exemptions, allowing federal and state agencies to use unregistered pesticides only to protect endangered species, quarantine invasive species, or protect public health.

analysis.who_pays: Agrochemical manufacturers that sell the eight named insecticides, and farmers — particularly in corn and soy — who would have to stop using treated seeds and spray products while the review proceeds. The bill's findings acknowledge that neonic seed coatings add little to soybean yields, but growers would still lose a familiar, inexpensive tool and could face pest pressure in the meantime.

drawbacks.text: The cancellation would take effect within 180 days of enactment, which is fast enough to disrupt growers mid-season and leave them without replacements against invasive pests, which is why the bill allows only narrow emergency exemptions.

The board could block pesticide registrations by a two-thirds vote and the EPA administrator would have to adopt its recommendation, shifting significant regulatory authority from the agency's normal scientific process to a new advisory body — and the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' in spending, with no dollar limit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health and food-supply benefits of protecting pollinators are large — bee losses were running at 35 to 46 percent a year, and one-third of North American food crops depend on bee pollination. The main costs fall on pesticide makers and on row-crop farmers who lose a cheap seed-treatment tool the EPA itself found adds little to soybean yields. The design is aggressive — a 180-day deadline and a new board with effective veto power over registrations — so the questions are less about whether the chemicals harm bees than about how abrupt and concentrated the review process would be.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Agriculture Committee — which never held a markup or scheduled it for the floor — from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Blumenauer introduced the bill on February 25, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Agriculture.
The Agriculture Committee referred it to its Subcommittee on Biotechnology, Horticulture, and Research on March 13, 2019, and no further action of any kind is recorded.
Eighty House members — the sponsor plus 79 cosponsors, all Democrats — supported the bill, but it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers and growers who rely on neonicotinoid-treated seeds kept using the chemicals, since the restriction never took effect and the pollinator review board was never created.

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the initial cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: 79 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Collin Peterson, D-MN)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee for the full two-year Congress — never scheduling a hearing or markup — and shunted it to the Subcommittee on Biotechnology, Horticulture, and Research two weeks after introduction.

against.name: Pesticide manufacturers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on neonicotinoid insecticides and defended their continued use in U.S. agriculture, in contrast to the European Union's outdoor ban on the same chemicals.

sides.party_line_note: All 79 cosponsors were Democrats and none of the chamber's 197 Republicans supported it, and the committee that buried the bill had a Democratic chair from a heavy corn-and-soy state.

industries.note: The bill would cancel the registrations of eight insecticides, including the neonicotinoids imidacloprid, clothianidin, and thiamethoxam, which are among the world's most widely used pesticides — a direct hit to revenue for companies like Bayer, Syngenta, and Corteva. Their interest in keeping the chemicals on the market runs against the beekeepers and consumers who absorb the cost of pollinator losses.

industries.industry: Row-crop farming and the treated-seed industry
industries.note: Corn and soy growers would lose access to neonicotinoid-coated seeds and spray treatments on bee-attractive plants. But the bill's own findings note that EPA determined neonic seed coatings provide little benefit to soybean yields and that the coatings are unnecessary in roughly 80 to 90 percent of row-crop uses, so growers would sacrifice little productive capacity while shedding an environmental cost.

Beekeepers lost 35 to 46 percent of hives annually between 2012 and 2018, according to the bill's findings, and the bill would give beekeepers three of the fifteen seats on the review board. Healthier pollinators directly protect their hives and their livelihood.

industries.industry: Fruit, vegetable, and nut growers dependent on pollination
industries.note: One-third of North American food production — including almonds, apples, avocados, and cranberries — depends on bee pollination, and native pollinators contribute over $3 billion to the agricultural economy. Stabilizing pollinator populations protects their crops.
